# What Do You Add? | Recommending the right next item when intent is already there


[Zepto Tech](https://medium.com/@tech.culture?source=post_page---byline--7a35a408b175-----------------------------------------)


9 min read


·


Just now


--


Press enter or click to view image in full size


You have almost certainly done this.


Your cart is at ₹340. Bread, milk, a bag of onions, a shampoo you were running low on. You are one tap from paying. And then you notice the line at the top of the screen: *add ₹59 more to unlock ₹75 off.*


So you do the arithmetic. If I add something for around ₹60 and save ₹75, the new item is effectively free. Better than free, actually. And it is not as though ₹60 of groceries goes to waste. There is always something the house needs.


That calculation is not a trick being played on you. Most of the time it is simply correct, and both sides come out ahead: you get more for less, and the order is worth more to us. This is one of the rare moments in commerce where the incentives genuinely point the same way.


And then you get stuck.


Press enter or click to view image in full size


Because knowing you *want* to add ₹59 of something is a completely different problem from knowing *what* . So you go back to browsing. You search for a couple of things half-heartedly. You scroll a category you had no intention of scrolling. Sometimes you find something. Often you give up, pay at ₹340, and leave the ₹75 on the table, mildly annoyed but not enough to do anything about it.


This is the part worth sitting with, because it is unusual. **The intent is already there.** The user is not being persuaded, not being sold to, not resisting. They have decided they are willing to spend a little more and are actively looking for a reason to. What stands between them and that purchase is not desire. It is a decision they cannot make quickly enough for it to be worth making.


Worse, the moment is fragile. Someone on the cart page is in checkout mode. They have finished shopping and are trying to leave. Sending them back into search or a category listing breaks that momentum, and momentum, once broken, frequently does not come back. Every second of browsing is a second in which the whole order is at risk, not just the ₹59.


So the question is narrow and quite hard: in a few seconds, on a page the user is trying to exit, what do you put in front of them?


## Why the obvious answer isn’t enough


The instinctive move is to find something priced at ₹59 and show it. That gets you part of the way, and no further.


The gap is not a fixed number. It is ₹59 for this user and ₹412 for the next, and the right answer looks nothing alike. Someone ₹59 away needs one well-chosen item. Someone ₹412 away is being asked to make a real decision about a real amount of money, and no quantity of ₹30 fillers gets them there in a way that feels like help rather than pressure.


Press enter or click to view image in full size


Price fit alone also produces absurd results. A ₹59 item the user would never buy is not a recommendation, it is noise. Their arithmetic does not stop running just because a coupon is dangling. Whatever we show still has to be something they actually want, at a price that still makes the maths work.


And the existing recommendation surfaces do not solve it either. Cart recommendations are usually built on similarity: you bought pasta, here is pasta sauce. That is a good answer to “what goes with this” and a poor answer to “what should I add to finish my order,” which is a different question with a price constraint attached to it.


What we needed was a recommendation that is *aware of where the user is standing* : how much is in the cart, how far the next milestone is, and what this particular person tends to buy. That awareness is the whole product.


## What belongs in the running


Recommendations are built in two stages: assemble a pool of plausible candidates, then rank them. Our pool draws on three different ideas about what might help, and the reason for three rather than one is that each covers a failure of the others.


Press enter or click to view image in full size


**Complementary items** are the familiar kind of recommendation: things that go with what is already in the basket. These are easy to say yes to, because the user has already demonstrated they want the thing it goes with. On their own, though, they tend to cluster around whatever dominates the cart, which is a problem when the cart is three unrelated things.


**Habitual items** come from the user’s own history. At checkout, the strongest predictor of what someone adds is what they always buy. These are the low-regret additions: no evaluation required, no risk of buying something that sits in the fridge untouched. Their weakness is that a person’s habits may contain nothing that fits the gap they happen to be facing.


One thing to note is that habit alone is not enough, though. The strongest signal that someone buys a product every week is also the reason not to show it to them the day after they bought it. A recommendation slot spent on rice somebody already has is a slot spent on nothing, and with only a handful of positions on the shelf, that is expensive. So repeat items are held back until enough of a user’s typical cycle has passed for the suggestion to be plausible again, and they return to contention as that moment approaches.

**Everyday top-ups** cover the rest. Some categories get added at the last moment far more often than others, not because they pair with anything specific but because they are small, useful and easy to decide on. We lean on those categories deliberately, shaped to each user rather than shown blindly, so a top-up suggestion is still something that person plausibly wants.


Together the three balance the qualities the moment demands: relevance to this cart, confidence from familiarity, and the small useful things that make closing a gap painless.


## How we rank them


This is where the problem becomes specific to the cart page, because ranking has to answer a question ordinary recommendation ranking never asks: *does the price of this item fit the gap?*


Every candidate is scored on three things. Two are conventional: how well it fits the current cart, and how much this user tends to like it. The third is built for this surface, and it is where most of the thinking went.


**Milestone Delta Score** measures the relationship between what a product costs and what the user still needs to spend. The scoring is deliberately asymmetric, because overshooting and undershooting fail in different ways and should not be punished the same.


An item that lands just above the gap is the ideal outcome. It closes the milestone in a single tap without spending much more than necessary, and the ranking chases that case hard.


An item that badly overshoots is penalised, and the more it overshoots the worse it does. Someone ₹59 short is not looking to spend ₹400. The wider the distance between what they need and what you are proposing, the more the recommendation reads as an upsell rather than a favour.


An item priced below the gap is the subtle case, and it is the one most systems get wrong by treating it as useless. It does not finish the job in one tap, so it cannot score perfectly. But plenty of these items are still genuinely good suggestions, and how good depends on how people actually buy them rather than on the shelf price alone. We score them accordingly, which means cheap items are neither dismissed nor allowed to crowd out better answers.


Press enter or click to view image in full size


The effect of all this is easiest to see where it overrules everything else. Imagine a user ₹50 short, and a loaf of bread that fits their cart perfectly and that they buy every single week. On any conventional recommendation ranking, bread wins outright. Here it comes second to a ₹55 pack of yoghurt they like slightly less, because that item ends the problem in one tap and the bread leaves them short. A recommendation engine with no sense of the gap would have got this backwards. That inversion is the entire reason the signal exists.


Press enter or click to view image in full size


One last pass enforces variety, so that a single category cannot take over the shelf and every position is doing different work.


## Small gaps and large gaps are different problems


The three signals are always present, but the balance between them shifts with the size of the gap. This turned out to matter more than almost anything else in the design.


When the gap is small, milestone delta score ** carries most of the weight. A user ₹50 from their milestone is in a solvable situation: there exists an item priced to close it that they also happen to want, and the job is simply to find that item. Relevance and personalisation still matter, but largely as tiebreakers among the many products that fit the price. Get this right and the interaction takes one tap.


When the gap is large, the balance deliberately tips the other way, toward relevance and personalisation, with milestone delta score pulled back.


Press enter or click to view image in full size


This is counterintuitive at first. A big gap needs a big-ticket item, so surely price fit should matter *more* ? In practice the opposite holds. Leaning hard on price fit at a large gap surfaces expensive products, and expensive products require consideration. Nobody researches a ₹400 purchase from a widget on the cart page while trying to check out. Recommend one and you get neither the add nor the goodwill.


So past a certain point we stop optimising for closing the gap and start optimising for something the user genuinely wants. The realistic goal changes: not one tap to the finish line, but real progress with a product they are happy to own. Some of those users reach the milestone over two or three additions. Some never reach it and still bought something they wanted, which is not a failure.


Put simply, a small gap is a pricing puzzle and a large gap is a recommendation problem. Treating both the same way is the most natural mistake to make here, and it is the one the weighting exists to prevent.


## How it helped


More users reached the milestone they were short of. The widget turned a question people were answering by browsing, or not answering at all, into something they could resolve in a tap or two without leaving the cart page, and a meaningfully larger share of them checked out with the coupon applied. That is the whole of what they wanted when they stopped to do the arithmetic.


Carts grew with them. Add-to-cart from the cart page rose, and because the items were ones people were glad to own rather than filler chosen to hit a number, average order value went up rather than simply shifting around. The additions were real demand that previously went unserved, not purchases moved from one surface to another.


Which is the unusual thing about this moment and the reason it was worth building for. The user wanted to spend a little more. We wanted the order to be worth a little more. Neither of us needed convincing, and all that stood in the way was a decision nobody had made easy. Answering the question they were already asking turned out to be the entire product.
